title: Snakebite: what NOT to do
asks: what not to do for a snake bite
should i suck the venom out of a snake bite
do i cut a snake bite
tourniquet for snake bite yes or no
should i put ice on a snakebite
does a snake bite kit or venom extractor work
can i take ibuprofen after a snake bite
should i kill the snake that bit me
tie off the arm above a snake bite?
snake bite, cut and suck or not, over
answer: Do not suck out the venom, by mouth or with a venom extractor or commercial snakebite kit.
Do not put on a tourniquet.

If a tourniquet or tight band is already on, do not take it off in the field: removing it can cause sudden collapse. The Joint Trauma System guideline says to leave it until medical staff are ready to treat and resuscitate the person.
Do not use electric shock, burning or chemicals on the bite.
Do not try to catch, kill or identify the snake. Do not touch its head even if it is dead or cut off: it can still bite.
Do not give alcohol or tobacco.
Do not break open blisters around the bite.
Do not touch your face or rub your eyes: venom may be on your hands and may cause blindness.
Do not take NSAID pain relievers such as ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin. Acetaminophen may be used.

Sources differ on tight bands and bandages. The Joint Trauma System snakebite guideline says do NOT apply constricting bandages: they may worsen tissue injury. The Army survival manual says to use a constricting band between the wound and the heart. WHO says a firm, broad pressure bandage may be used: it is recommended where local snakes cause nerve damage, paralysis or severe illness, or where transport will be long, and NOT recommended where the venom mainly damages tissue near the bite without body-wide symptoms.
warnings: Cutting causes unnecessary bleeding and opens a direct route into the blood for venom and infection.
If venom gets into damaged tissue in your mouth, you could lose consciousness or even die.
A tourniquet or ice is not effective and can cause additional harm.

quotes.text: 1. DO NOT cut, suck, electrocute, burn, or use chemicals on the envenomation site. 2. DO NOT apply constricting bandages, tourniquets, or other circulation-reducing intervention! 3. DO NOT use venom extractors or other commercial snakebite ﬁrst aid kits.
DO NOT attempt to cut open the bite or suck out the venom. If the venom should seep through any damaged or lacerated tissues in your mouth, you could immediately lose consciousness or even die.
DO NOT put a tourniquet around the snake bite or limb. • DO NOT cut the bite out as this will lead to unnecessary bleeding. • DO NOT suck on the bite to remove the venom.
If a tourniquet is already in place, see Tourniquet Algorithm. Do not remove it until you are ready to treat and resuscitate the patient as a rapid decompensation can occur.
Tourniquets and constricting bands may worsen snakebite outcomes and must be removed according to the Tourniquet Algorithm.
Cleanse the wound gently with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Do not apply ice or use a TQ, as they are not effective and can cause additional harm.
Don’t try to ID the snake. You don’t need to know the snake’s species to treat the patient. Trying to catch or kill the snake is dangerous and wastes time.
In the event you are bitten, do not attempt to identify and or kill the snake. Freshly killed snakes can continue to bite due to reflexive action. Snake identification is not critical.
DO NOT take risks to obtain photos! Never touch the head with your hands - even a decapitated snake head can bite and inject venom >24 hours after the bite.

Do not— • Give the victim or take alcoholic beverages or tobacco products, or administer atropine, morphine or other central nervous system depressors. • Make any deep cuts at the bite site. Cutting opens capillaries that in turn open a direct route into the blood stream for venom and infection. • Put the hands on the face or rub the eyes, as venom may be on hands. Venom may cause blindness. • Break open the large blisters that form around the bite site.

Ketamine and fentanyl are preferable for analgesia. Histamine release from morphine may mimic signs of an allergic reaction or worsen hypotension. Acetaminophen may be used but NSAIDs are contraindicated.
Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac.

Aspirin, an NSAID, and acetaminophen, an analgesic and antipyretic, both lower body core temperature by normalizing the elevated hypothalamic set point that regulates the fever response caused by pyrogens
DO NOT apply constricting bandages or tourniquets as these may worsen local tissue injury and increase the risk of permanent disability.
Use a constricting band between the wound and the heart.

You may choose to use a broad pressure bandage and wrap upwards from the lower portion of the bite. The bandage should be firm, but should not cut off pulses in the limb. Extend the bandage as high up the limb as possible. –– This is recommended if the snakes in your area produce a toxin that damages the nerves, causes paralysis, causes the person to become very ill or if there will be prolonged transport time. –– This is NOT recommended if the snakes in your area produce toxins that primarily cause tissue damage near the wound and do not cause body-wide symptoms.

conflict: Constricting bands and pressure bandages: JTS Snakebite CPG (2026) says 'DO NOT apply constricting bandages, tourniquets, or other circulation-reducing intervention'; Army ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 'Use a constricting band between the wound and the heart'; WHO BEC (2018) allows a broad pressure bandage, recommended only where local snakes cause nerve damage or paralysis, severe illness, or transport is prolonged, and NOT recommended where venom mainly causes tissue damage near the wound; ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says to bandage 'snug but not too tight'. All agree: no tourniquet. The card shows the three positions in one line; the owner must choose. A tourniquet or band that is already on: JTS says not to remove it until ready to treat and resuscitate; its Tourniquet Algorithm is a figure with no extractable text, so the kit gives no removal steps and no time limit; the owner should confirm the 'leave it on' wording for long evacuations. NSAIDs: the JTS snakebite sentence ('NSAIDs are contraindicated') is from its supportive-care section, written for medical providers, and names no drugs; the examples come from the JTS Traumatic Brain Injury CPG (2017: 'NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac') and TB MED 507 (2022: 'Aspirin, an NSAID'), both written about other conditions. The JTS Frostbite CPG sentence that names ibuprofen and aspirin was not used because it recommends them (for frostbite pain) and would read the wrong way on this card. Minor: ATP 3-50.21 also says not to administer atropine or morphine (JTS uses atropine for some neurotoxic bites and prefers ketamine or fentanyl to morphine); these provider-level points are not in the card. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) and FEMA P-2064 (2020) were searched: neither covers snakebite treatment.

review.notes: Re-review of the revised card (full check). Fixed: A4 existing tourniquet stays on (JTS, attributed); A11 now names the drugs: 'Do not take NSAID pain relievers such as ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin. Acetaminophen may be used.' The drug examples come from JTS TBI CPG ('NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac') and TB MED 507 ('Aspirin, an NSAID'), written about other conditions, but they only establish class membership, which does not depend on the condition, so there is no meaning drift; the drafter was right not to use the JTS Frostbite sentence that recommends those drugs. A7 adds the do-not-touch-the-head line (JTS). Same 'leave it on' judgement as snakebite-first-aid: ACCEPTABLE to show, attributed, with the conflict note that the kit gives no time limit. All other don'ts confirmed in batch 1. No PDF junk. Asks all answered, including ibuprofen and tie-off.
